reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours of the CNS
clinicalPearls: A benign, highly vascular tumour (CNS WHO grade 1) most often located in the cerebellum, but also the brainstem and spinal cord
The commonest primary intra-axial posterior fossa tumour in adults and a defining lesion of von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease
Classically appears on MRI as a cystic lesion with an intensely enhancing mural nodule
Tumour cells can produce erythropoietin, causing secondary polycythaemia in a proportion of patients
Multiple or early-onset haemangioblastomas should prompt evaluation for germline VHL mutation and associated tumours
Histology shows abundant thin-walled capillaries interspersed with lipid-laden stromal cells, the neoplastic component
Surgical resection of the mural nodule is usually curative for solitary sporadic tumours
reference.pathophysiology: Haemangioblastoma is a benign, highly vascular neoplasm whose neoplastic element is the interstitial stromal cell, set within a rich network of capillaries. It arises most commonly in the cerebellum and also in the brainstem, spinal cord and retina. Inactivation of the VHL tumour-suppressor gene, whether germline in von Hippel-Lindau disease or somatic in sporadic tumours, leads to stabilisation of hypoxia-inducible factors and upregulation of angiogenic and erythropoietic signalling. This drives the characteristic vascularity and, through erythropoietin production, can cause secondary polycythaemia. Cyst formation with a mural nodule is typical, and mass effect on the cerebellum or brainstem produces the clinical features.
additionalDifferentials: Metastasis (e.g. renal cell carcinoma, itself VHL-associated)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced brain and spinal MRI to characterise the cyst and enhancing mural nodule and detect multiple lesions
Full blood count to detect secondary polycythaemia
Germline VHL genetic testing when disease is multiple, early-onset or familial
Screening for VHL-associated tumours (renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, pancreatic and retinal lesions)
Histopathology showing stromal cells within a capillary-rich matrix
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging posterior fossa cyst with obstructive hydrocephalus
Brainstem compression or new bulbar signs
Multiple lesions or associated tumours indicating VHL disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent for solitary sporadic tumours, which are usually cured by complete surgical excision of the mural nodule. Patients with von Hippel-Lindau disease develop multiple lesions over time and require lifelong surveillance, with morbidity arising from recurrent tumours and associated systemic neoplasms.
pitfalls: Failing to recognise the VHL association and missing multiple or systemic tumours
Underestimating the marked vascularity and risk of intraoperative haemorrhage
Overlooking secondary polycythaemia as a clue to the diagnosis
Mistaking a solitary cerebellar metastasis for haemangioblastoma or vice versa
references: WHO Classification of Tumours of the Central Nervous System
Louis DN et al. The 2021 WHO Classification of Tumors of the Central Nervous System
management: Complete microsurgical excision of the enhancing mural nodule, which is curative for solitary sporadic tumours
Offer stereotactic radiosurgery for small, multiple or surgically inaccessible lesions, particularly in von Hippel-Lindau disease
Consider the HIF-2-alpha inhibitor belzutifan for von Hippel-Lindau-associated haemangioblastomas not amenable to local treatment
Manage peritumoural oedema and mass effect with corticosteroids and treat obstructive hydrocephalus or raised intracranial pressure from posterior fossa lesions as a neurosurgical emergency
Address secondary polycythaemia driven by erythropoietin production, with venesection where required
Undertake germline VHL testing and offer genetic counselling and family screening for multiple, early-onset or familial disease
Enrol von Hippel-Lindau patients in lifelong surveillance for renal cell carcinoma, phaeochromocytoma, pancreatic and retinal lesions, with serial neuraxial MRI and ophthalmological review
